title: The Green Journal of Hesper
subtitle: Nine chapters from an orbital farm whose only plant speaks in leaves
author: scriptaWorlds · ALA
dedication: For the ones whose names were cut out at the binding.
preface:
## Preface

Hesper is a farm: a root ring, a work ring and a low ring strung on a spine in orbit, forty-one people, stores that come up from the surface on manifests, and one plant.

That plant fills the root wall and it holds the station's air. It has no voice. It speaks with its leaves, which bend into drawn shapes, and the shapes are read by a child — the Reader — because a child reads a shape whole, while an adult reads the letters he was taught and stops there.

Whatever the plant is read as asking for is granted within three days, and the request is written into the green journal, one dated line in the officer's hand. A line that is not kept costs the hand that wrote it a tooth, then a finger, then an eye. There has never been a fourth day, so nobody on Hesper knows what follows an eye, and the farm says so the way it says the air pressure.

This book is nine chapters of that arithmetic. It opens on a third morning, with three arms lying unbandaged in the infirmary because the plant has not stopped shaking, and it follows what a small crew does when the only instrument it has for its own survival is a page of drawn shapes and a child who can read them and cannot read anything else.

The Green Journal of Hesper is not a story about a monster in the soil, and it is not a story about a rebellion. It is about a farm that must answer something every single day, with water and light and warmth and, sometimes, with blood; about a doctor who keeps a column of numbers on an infirmary wall because that column is the only honest record of what the farm has actually done; about an officer who was punished as a boy and has been careful ever since; about an old man who drew the chart of signs and then stopped reading them; about an engineer who counts the register's holes; and about a mother who has worked the second shift for nine years so as not to stand under the flower.

What the book is after is narrower than a war and harder than one. It asks what a request means when the one who makes it cannot be asked back; what a rule is worth when nothing enforces it except the habit of the people who keep it; and what a farm owes the children it has already spent. Every chapter here is a consequence of a single law, stated at the front of the story and never broken: the plant asks, the farm answers, and the answer is measured in what the farm can see.

Read it the way the crew reads its own wall. The days are dated, the readings are in the doctor's hand, and the two things that never stop running — the count in the book and the column on the wall — will tell you where you are.
afterword:
## Afterword

Hesper keeps two records of the same thing. One is the green journal, where a request becomes a line, and the line, once written, becomes the debt of the hand that wrote it. The other is a column of numbers on the infirmary wall, where a doctor writes down what the air actually did. The two are never quite the same, and this book was built to stand in the gap between them: between what a farm says it has done and what its instruments can show.

Nine chapters is short for a station that measures its own history in flowerings nine years apart. What the book leaves with the reader, instead of a long chronicle, is a set of instruments and the people who read them: a child who reads drawn shapes whole and cannot read a written word; a chart drawn by an adult whose strokes once turned light into blood; a register with whole years cut out at the binding; a rule made at the wall with no line under it, so that nothing enforces it but the crew's own habit of keeping it.

If there is an argument here, it is about what an answer is. A plant that speaks in leaves cannot be asked what it meant, and a farm that lives on its air cannot wait for certainty. So the characters in this book do the only thing available to them, which is to choose what to measure and then live with the number. Some of them measure blood. One of them measures the water. The Reader measures the shape, and the child's advantage is not innocence, it is attention.

This edition is a working record rather than a monument: three weeks of a flowering and the mornings that came after it, in the order the farm lived them. Read it the way Verrin reads the soil — slowly, and with your hands.
